_comment: Phase 18D: small, flat-chance positive events — deliberately simpler than data/events.json (no exposure/mitigation modeling). Rolled once per player per year (src/engine/events/positiveEvents.ts). Rewards are flat regardless of realm size by design: this is flavor, not a strategy lever, so it stays small relative to a mature economy while still meaning something early. "some funny ones as well" per the playtest request that asked for this.

events.text: A traveling merchant arrives with the exact sum owed from three winters past, paid without a word of apology.
A traveling merchant sells his entire cart of Flemish cloth at your market — better prices than he expected, and he remembers who to thank.
A traveling merchant barters half his cargo against a short-term loan from your treasury. He repays it the same afternoon, with interest.
A traveling merchant, grateful for safe passage through your roads, leaves a share of his profits at the gate.
A passing tax collector, distracted by his ledgers, pays the same road toll twice. The gate-keeper keeps half and dutifully presents the rest.
A passing tax collector, mistaking your steward for a merchant, agrees to a one-time levy arrangement that leaves your treasury rather fuller.
A passing tax collector arrives to audit the region and departs satisfied — though rather more coin stays in your hands than he intended.
A visiting bishop, travelling with a large retinue, pays your road toll twice — the second time out of habit, and he does not ask for it back.
A visiting bishop holds a sermon in your chapel and takes up a collection. He forgets to take the collection with him.
A visiting bishop spends a night in the castle and departs in haste, leaving a leather purse tucked between the mattresses.
A retired soldier, clearly still following old marching routes, pays the road toll twice without noticing. He seems pleased to be following a schedule.
A retired soldier, grateful for the peace your rule has kept, donates his mustering pay to the treasury. It is more than expected.
A retired soldier, stopping for the night, forgets a purse at the garrison — found the next morning after he has already marched on.
A grateful pilgrim feasts at the roadside inn, pronounces the bread the finest in the empire, and leaves coin enough to prove it.
A grateful pilgrim repays a debt contracted by your predecessor — a small thing in its time, rather more coin now.
A grateful pilgrim, refreshed by your roads and your wells, leaves behind a coin purse at the chapel door. No note; presumably God keeps the accounts.
A wandering minstrel performs in your market square and draws the largest crowd in memory. He tips your gate-keeper generously; your gate-keeper tips you.
A wandering minstrel, recalling a favor done to his father by your predecessor, insists on settling the debt in coin rather than song.
A wandering minstrel reports your roads are the smoothest in three provinces and recommends them loudly. A small purse arrives from a grateful innkeeper's guild.
A shrewd moneylender calls in an old note — one your treasury holds, not his. He pays, grimly, in full.
A shrewd moneylender repays a loan your predecessor made decades ago. He waited until the interest exceeded the principal, then paid only the principal. Still coin.
A shrewd moneylender, reassured by your stable roads and courts, extends credit at a preferential rate. The arrangement fee stays in your hands.
A returning trade caravan carries a payment long overdue from a Venetian factor. Three provinces to deliver it, and they did.
A returning trade caravan offloads surplus stock at your market — more than they planned to sell, at better prices than they expected.
A returning trade caravan strikes a compact with your grain merchants: grain now, Flemish goods in the spring. The advance lands in your treasury today.
A minor noble passing through stops to settle a matter of honour — specifically, a debt of honour owed to your house since before you held it.
A minor noble passing through sells off a cartload of silver plate, eager for coin. Your merchant gets first offer.
A minor noble passing through wants a letter of safe passage and is willing to overpay for it. You oblige.
A minor noble passing through, noting the clean roads and the absence of bandits, leaves a small gift at your gate. It is the right kind of small.
A guild of tanners passes through with three carts of hides. The toll-keeper counts each cart twice. The tanners do not review the receipt.
A guild of tanners negotiates a season's exclusive right to sell in your market. The exclusivity fee is paid upfront.
A guild of tanners, grateful for your market ordinances that keep foreign hides out, sends a purse to express their appreciation.
A fishing fleet returning from a long season pays the harbour toll twice — once for the voyage, once for the catch. The second payment is accepted without comment.
A fishing fleet, sitting on a surplus season with nowhere to sell, offers a tenth of the catch's value to your treasury in exchange for market access.
A fishing fleet captain, celebrating a record season at your taverns, leaves a coin purse with the innkeeper. It finds its way to you.
A traveling notary, thorough to a fault, pays the road toll twice and files both receipts. No refund is requested or issued.
A traveling notary, drawing up your estate records, discovers a clerical omission worth correcting — in your favour.
A traveling notary, rushing to make his next appointment, forgets his fee purse at the registry office. A week passes before anyone sends word.
A cousin twice removed, arriving uninvited for a fortnight, departs with uncharacteristic grace and leaves a purse behind. Nobody asks questions.
A cousin twice removed turns up to repay money borrowed in your grandfather's time. The note was lost. He remembered it anyway.
A cousin twice removed, unaccountably in good humor, presses coin into your steward's hand on the way out the gate.
A vineyard owner hosts your court for an afternoon tasting and includes a cash gift alongside the wine. The wine is adequate.
A vineyard owner settles a loan your family made after a bad harvest, three decades back. The interest is substantial.
A vineyard owner, grateful for your roads' effect on his shipping costs, pays a voluntary toll at the season's end. His accountant is baffled; you are not.
A cartwright delivers both a new cart and the full sum owed for the last repair order. The cart is better than expected. So is the settlement.
A cartwright repays a workshop loan ahead of schedule, with a note that your interest rates are fair. The note does not add to the sum.
A cartwright, whose wheels last twice as long on your roads as anywhere else, sends a modest annual appreciation. It arrives reliably.
A wool merchant, returning from the eastern fair, delivers settlement on three seasons of credit — short only by road costs, which he waives.
A wool merchant, finding your market thick with buyers, sells out before noon and tips the gate-keeper enough that word travels.
A wool merchant secures your principality as first stop on next year's circuit, paying the preference in coin.
A family of weavers, fleeing a guild dispute in the next province, arrives with three looms and no intention of leaving.
A family of weavers moves in, then sends word back. Three more households follow before the month is out.
A family of weavers, courted by two other lords, chooses your principality for reasons they decline to specify but clearly involve the tax rate.
A band of hardy farmers, displaced by a landlord's enclosure, pitches camp at the edge of your farmland and asks to stay. You see no reason to refuse.
A band of hardy farmers, settled for barely one season, sends for the rest of their village. They are all here by autumn.
A band of hardy farmers arrives asking about soil and markets. They like both answers and begin planting.
A group of skilled masons, finishing a contract to the north, hears that work is plentiful here and stops rather than moving on.
A group of skilled masons settles in and, within a year, has talked a dozen families from their old home into making the same move.
A group of skilled masons comes looking for steady contracts and finds them. They build a house before they have finished unloading.
Word of your fair rule reaches a family in the next valley, who arrive before your messenger does.
Word of your fair rule spreads through three market towns. By the following spring, a steady trickle has become a flow.
Word of your fair rule travels further than your couriers do. A dozen new families arrive before anyone thought to count them.
A small caravan of refugees, moving through your roads, asks to stop for the winter. By spring they have put down roots.
A small caravan of refugees stops in the market town and is astonished to find their coin worth something here. They send letters. More come.
A small caravan of refugees, expecting little, finds full markets and a fair magistrate. They write home immediately.
A traveling blacksmith and his kin arrive, set up the forge, and tell their cousins. The cousins arrive with more cousins.
A traveling blacksmith and his kin settle in your quarter, and within the year the whole street knows them — along with several families who followed their recommendation.
A traveling blacksmith and his kin find your market town exactly what they were looking for, and stop moving.
A cheerful young couple settles near the mill, starts a family, and seems to attract other cheerful young couples by some natural law.
A cheerful young couple, offered land in three provinces, chooses yours. They say the roads are better. The roads are not especially better.
A troupe of craftsmen, drifting after a long contract, hears your building projects need workers and decides to stay permanently.
A troupe of craftsmen moves in together, takes up a row of houses, and within a season has imported most of their extended families.
A troupe of craftsmen, offered terms by two rival lords, chooses yours. Afterward, they explain it came down to the bread at the market.
News of your prosperity reaches three provinces away. One family in ten takes it as a recommendation.
News of your prosperity convinces a whole hamlet to uproot. They arrive well-organized and immediately begin improving the road they came in on.
News of your prosperity draws settlers the way a good harvest draws crows — reliably, and in numbers.
A group of shepherds, following the flock to better pasture, realizes your land is better than most and makes it permanent.
A group of shepherds persuades a whole hamlet to follow their flock. They all arrive together, with the sheep, in early spring.
A group of shepherds arrives looking for grazing rights and stays to build a proper house.
A midwife's exceptional year — twelve healthy births, no losses — becomes the talk of neighboring villages.
A midwife's good year draws expectant families from across the region, some of whom simply never leave.
A midwife's good year becomes common knowledge. Several families move here specifically because of it.
A returning group of your own emigrants comes back, having tried elsewhere and found it wanting. They bring new skills and a chastened appreciation.
A returning group of your own emigrants is the talk of the market for a week. Their homecoming convinces several fence-sitters to stop sitting.
A returning group of your own emigrants, having lived in two other principalities, declares yours preferable without qualification.
A family fleeing a harsher lord arrives with everything they own on a cart, asks nothing, and unpacks immediately.
A family fleeing a harsher lord becomes a local cause. Three more families from the same village arrive within the month.
A family fleeing a harsher lord finds your markets open and your laws clear. They send a letter back. It is not a discouraging letter.
A pair of newlyweds arrives, looks around, and concludes this is a fine place to start. A year later the household has doubled.
A pair of newlyweds, comparing three principalities on their way south, picks yours without much debate and moves in.
A neighboring miller, sitting on more grain than his cellars can hold, sells the excess to your granary before it turns.
A neighboring miller, reviewing his accounts, finds a season's deliveries were under-counted. The corrected figure fills your barns.
A neighboring miller swaps a debt of neighborly goodwill for grain — your barns get the better end of the arrangement.
A neighboring miller, in an unusual fit of civic spirit, sends a tithe of his surplus to your stores unasked.
A grateful village, in a year when their harvest outran their needs, sends a wagonload of wheat to the granary. No obligation; just neighborliness.
A grateful village, remembering your help with the last drought, delivers a cartload of good wheat as thanks.
A grateful village, excavating an old storage cellar, finds a forgotten reserve still sound and sends the best of it your way.
An old grain store, sealed and unlogged for two winters, is opened and found to contain sound wheat. A portion finds its way to the treasury barns.
An old grain store was under-counted at the last audit. The corrected measure adds meaningfully to the reserve.
An old grain store, included in a trade arrangement most people had forgotten about, delivers its due years late but intact.
An old grain store attached to a dissolved monastery defaults to your administration. Most of it is still edible.
A traveling monk, traveling with his order's surplus, deposits a wagonload at your granary as a charitable deed. His order has many such wagonloads.
A traveling monk, housed and fed for a week at your inn, sends a cartload of rye from his abbey as thanks.
A traveling monk, staying at a derelict priory, finds a hidden grain cellar whose existence everyone had forgotten. He sends word; your men retrieve most of it.
A passing quartermaster, traveling with army surplus after a campaign that ended early, sells the extra grain to your stores rather than haul it home.
A passing quartermaster, re-examining his manifests, finds a wagonload of rye that was never logged. He sells it here rather than explain it later.
A passing quartermaster trades grain from a cancelled provisioning order against your help with lodging. The grain is the better end of the deal.
A passing quartermaster, grateful for your roads and your wells, releases a portion of his surplus to your granary at no charge.
A returning harvest crew, paid partly in grain, sells the bulk to your barns on the way through rather than carry it further.
A returning harvest crew, sheltered during a storm at your expense, sends several sacks of the season's wheat as thanks the following week.
A returning harvest crew, sheltering in a disused barn, discovers a cache of dried grain behind the rear wall. They report it; you claim it.
A charitable abbey, overflowing from a good harvest, sends three cartloads of rye to your stores as a gesture of fraternal abundance.
A charitable abbey, reviewing its tithes, discovers it has been underdelivering your portion for two seasons. The corrected tally is paid in full.
A charitable abbey trades its surplus against toll-free passage for its pilgrims. The grain is real; the pilgrims don't cost you much.
A charitable abbey, in a year of exceptional harvest, elects to send double the usual tithe without being asked.
A friendly rival ruler, hedging against a bad harvest of his own, sells you a wagonload of grain at a price that implies he trusts you.
A friendly rival ruler sends several sacks of grain with a diplomatic note — good wheat, no strings, a gesture worth taking at face value.
A friendly rival ruler, cleaning out an old garrison, finds grain still sound and offers it at a price that implies he just wants it gone.
A retired granary keeper, visited for old times' sake, confesses he kept a private reserve 'for emergencies' in a corner bin. He donates it.
A retired granary keeper, in declining health and a confessional mood, reveals he had been under-counting deliveries for years. It all comes to you now.
A retired granary keeper, called back as a consultant, finds discrepancies that work out in your favor, and asks for nothing but an acknowledgment.
A retired granary keeper, grateful for the pension your administration continued, donates a season's personal reserve to the granary.
A well-stocked mill, bursting at the end of a busy season, sells the overflow to your barns before the rains come.
A well-stocked mill, catching the season's last good wheat, sets aside a portion for your granary as a standing gesture of goodwill.
A well-stocked mill, extending the cellar, breaks through into a sealed older chamber. The grain inside is mostly still good.
A well-timed festival fills the market square with music and the smell of roasting. For one day, the principality forgets it has problems.
A well-timed festival gives the grumblers something better to do with the afternoon than grumble.
A well-timed festival puts the whole town in one square, which is the only reliable way to make neighbors stop feuding.
A well-timed festival reminds even the most contrary of your subjects that they chose to live here.
A local wedding, celebrated with more enthusiasm than the family expected to afford, lifts the whole quarter's mood for a week.
A local wedding is an occasion for peace — old disputes set aside, free ale on the house, and nobody looking for trouble.
A local wedding pulls three feuding families into the same courtyard. They eat, they drink, they forget what the feud was about.
A local wedding is done properly, and the whole town agrees: this is how things ought to be done here.
A good rumor about the harvest — three parts true, one part wishful — gives the market a week of optimism.
A good rumor about the harvest travels faster than any official report and improves everyone's mood in advance of the actual result.
A good rumor about the harvest arrives precisely when grumbling was turning into something worse.
A good rumor about the harvest turns a dreary market week into a sociable one.
A traveling storyteller sets up in the inn and draws a crowd every night for a week. The town is noticeably more cheerful when he leaves.
A traveling storyteller tells a tale everyone repeats for days — a story about a principality, oddly, a great deal like this one.
A traveling storyteller arrives at the moment when the market mood needed turning. He turns it.
A minor tax dispute, long festering, is settled in public by your magistrate with unmistakable fairness. The crowd watching takes note.
A minor tax dispute is resolved clearly and promptly. The decision does not go entirely one party's way, but everyone agrees it was handled rightly.
A minor tax dispute, resolved publicly and fairly, gives the town something to feel good about — which is not a common outcome in tax cases.
A minor tax dispute becomes a minor public triumph when your court decides it correctly and everyone knows it.
An unexpected holiday is declared — the occasion is forgotten by evening, but the festival continues regardless.
An unexpected holiday gives the whole town an afternoon off. It is remarkable how much goodwill one free afternoon buys.
An unexpected holiday, proclaimed on short notice, is greeted with the kind of enthusiasm that implies people were ready for one.
An unexpected holiday, given without obvious occasion, reminds people that the ruler sometimes acts without being asked.
A popular local wrestler takes the prize at the regional fair. The town celebrates for three days as though they had won something themselves.
A popular local team wins the archery contest at the regional fair. The story improves with each telling and is still improving.
A popular local victory at the fair gives the town something to celebrate instead of something to complain about.
A popular local victory at the fair turns what had been a dull autumn into a memorable one.
A well-loved priest delivers the sermon everyone will remember for years. The crowd leaves in noticeably better spirits.
A well-loved priest's sermon is the talk of the market for a week, and not in a troublesome way.
A well-loved priest's sermon lands precisely where it needs to — on the people who most needed to hear it.
A round of free ale at the tavern, sponsored by no one anyone will admit to, lifts the mood of the whole quarter.
A round of free ale at the tavern smooths over a week's worth of petty irritations in a single evening.
A round of free ale at the tavern is the most efficient peacemaking tool in the medieval world, and tonight it earns its reputation.
A round of free ale at the tavern, free for one evening only, generates more goodwill than three civic announcements.
A juggler passing through town sets up in the square and draws a crowd. Even the toll-keeper comes out to watch.
A juggler passing through town provides an hour of distraction at precisely the right moment — when distraction was what the town most needed.
A juggler passing through town draws the whole market square into one place, which turns into a party by mid-afternoon.
A juggler passing through town declares, loudly and often, that your market is his favorite stop on the whole route.
A rare clear night draws everyone onto their rooftops to stare at the stars. No one can explain why this improves things, but it does.
A rare clear night for stargazing has the whole town trading opinions about constellations and omens — the good kind of omen, for once.
A rare clear night gives even the grumbliest of your subjects a reason to stand still and look upward instead of sideways.
A rare clear night turns a dull winter week into an occasion. Someone builds a bonfire; it spreads from there.
A surprise reunion of old friends fills the inn to capacity and spills into the square. The whole town shares in it, even if only in the noise.
A surprise reunion of old friends becomes the event of the season. People who were not there describe it to people who were.
A surprise reunion of old friends happens to coincide with a week when the town was on a short fuse. The reunion wins.
A traveling salesman insists your castle needs a slightly bigger flag. You decline; he tips out of embarrassment.
Someone finally pays back the Baron who ruled three reigns ago. You were not expecting this.
A rival's messenger delivers a bribe to the wrong address. Yours.
A traveling dentist sets up shop, does brisk business, and leaves a "thank you" donation.
Your court jester wins a bet with a visiting noble. He shares the winnings, mostly.
A merchant caravan mistakes your border for a toll road that stopped existing decades ago. They pay anyway.
An anonymous benefactor leaves a sack of coin at the gate with a note reading simply "well governed."
A traveling astrologer predicts your prosperity, and several nobles pay handsomely to hear it confirmed.
Your scribes discover a clerical error that has been quietly costing the Kaiser money and not you.
A duel over a card game ends peacefully, and the loser insists on paying your treasury instead of his opponent.
A famous chef relocates to your lands purely for the produce. His apprentices follow within the year.
A traveling theater troupe likes it here so much they simply never leave.
Twins are born in the same week to three different families. Word travels; more families arrive hoping for luck.
A minor prophecy names your principality "a good place to raise children." People take it seriously.
A beekeeper's spectacular honey harvest becomes regional gossip, and with it, your reputation.
An old hermit comes down from the hills, likes what he sees, and tells everyone he knows. He knows a lot of people.
A visiting friar blesses the harvest. The harvest, coincidentally or not, turns out slightly better than expected.
A miller's scale was broken for months, undercounting deliveries. It is fixed, and the barns are fuller than the books claimed.
A rival principality's granary roof collapses. They sell the contents cheap rather than let it spoil, and you buy in.
A field thought exhausted produces one unexpectedly generous crop before finally giving out.
A traveling comedian performs in the square and the whole town is still laughing about it a week later.
A pig escapes the market and leads half the town on a chase. Nobody catches it, but everyone has a good story now.
Two feuding families settle their dispute over ale instead of at the gallows, to general relief.
A local legend turns out to be true, or at least everyone agrees to believe it is. Morale improves regardless.
The tavern keeper announces a "harvest special" and, for one evening, nobody complains about anything.
A traveling bard writes a song about your realm. It is not entirely accurate, but it is very catchy.
A stray dog adopts the guardhouse. Morale among the guards — and by extension everyone else — noticeably improves.
A minor miracle is reported at the local chapel. Investigation is inconclusive; enthusiasm is not.
The weather clears just in time for a long-planned market day, and everyone remembers it fondly for months.
A visiting acrobat troupe puts on an unscheduled show in the square. Even the tax collector stops to watch.
